To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the intake of an imperfect substitute can affect the slope of the demand curve for the complementary element of food and (2) an imperfect substitute can reduce intake of the complementary element of the food without affecting the slope of the food demand curve.

the availability of a perfect substitute for food (i.e. saccharin) does not reduce food intake in monkeys, whereas the availability of an imperfect substitute (i.e. sucrose) reduces food intake in rats.
increases in the fixed ratios of presses required for food or sucrose pellets reduced the food intake of monkeys and rats but did not affect the intake of the sucrose or saccharin solution.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of substitution and regulation on the control of food intake.

the effect of a complementary element of food on the demand for food in the absence and presence of a complementary element and with the regulation of body weight and daily intake of food and the complementary element.
the effect of a substitute for food on the demand for food in rats and monkeys.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
rats and monkeys defend their total daily caloric intake and that the defense of intake is accomplished by regulating intake of the complementary elements of food.
the rats and monkeys increased their daily output in the presence of the imperfect substitutes and thereby defended their respective daily intakes of the complementary elements of the food.
, in a closed economy, an imperfect substitute for a complementary element of food can reduce the demand for that element.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the intake of a substitute for food is regulated, but that the demand for food is not.

, when the fixed ratio of responses per reinforcer is increased, demand for the reinforcer is reduced and, if a complementary element of food is available, the intake of the complementary element is reduced.

the use of food substitutes can be a useful tool in the development of demand curves in animals.
rats and monkeys can defend their caloric intake in an environment where they have a choice between two complementary sources of calories.
